title: Straight into the desert (Mark 1:9–13)
hook: baptism, the voice, then the Spirit drives him out among the wild beasts

segments.voice: Yesterday, the beginning of Mark, and the word gospel. Your line was gospel means good news. Today, Jesus walks into the story.

Some storytellers linger. They give you the weather, the smell of the kitchen, what everyone was wearing. Not Mark. Mark is the friend who tells a story so fast you have to say, wait, back up. In five verses today, Jesus arrives from a small village, is baptized in a river, sees the sky rip open, hears a voice, and is driven out into the wilderness for forty days. Mark has a favorite word for this speed, and you're going to start hearing it everywhere.
screen: `SOME STORYTELLERS LINGER.` → `MARK DOES NOT.` → `FIVE VERSES, FORTY DAYS.`

segments.voice: First, the river. Jesus comes from Nazareth in Galilee, and John baptizes him in the Jordan. Mark doesn't stop to explain why. He just moves. Second, the word. In the Douay-Rheims: "And forthwith coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens opened, and the Spirit as a dove descending, and remaining on him." Forthwith. Older English Bibles say straightway. In Greek it's euthys, immediately, right then. Mark reaches for it again and again, and it gives his whole gospel the feeling of running. Third, the sky. Where the English says opened, Mark's Greek actually says the heavens were torn, ripped like cloth. And a voice from heaven says: you are my beloved Son, in you I am well pleased. Catholics see the whole Trinity in this moment: the Son in the water, the Spirit like a dove, the Father's voice. Fourth, the desert. Then, immediately again: "And immediately the Spirit drove him out into the desert." Drove is a strong word, the same word Mark later uses for driving out demons. Jesus is there forty days, tempted by Satan, with the wild beasts, and angels serve him. Mark gives it one sentence. He doesn't tell us what the temptations were; Matthew and Luke do that. Mark leaves them untold, and adds a detail of his own: the wild beasts. Beloved, and straight into the wilderness: in Mark, being loved by God doesn't mean an easy road. It means the road starts right away.
screen: `FROM NAZARETH TO THE JORDAN.` · `EUTHYS: STRAIGHTWAY.` · `THE HEAVENS TORN OPEN.` · `DRIVEN INTO THE WILDERNESS.` · then, large: `THE SPIRIT DROVE HIM OUT INTO THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: Replay your morning quickly: woke up, and straightway, phone; straightway, coffee; straightway, the next thing; and notice how few pauses there were. Now, for these two minutes, don't go straightway anywhere; stay put. If you pray, rest in the word spoken over Jesus at the river, beloved; if you don't, just rest.
Euthys. Mark's favorite Greek word, straightway, immediately, carrying Jesus from the river to the wilderness in a single breath, his baptism and his forty days. Today's word.
Your line: straightway. Mark's favorite word, and he won't slow down. Day one hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Baptism of the Lord as the feast that closes the Christmas season, and hear Mark's short account of the forty days in the desert on the First Sunday of Lent in Year B.

original.note: Greek: straightway, immediately, Mark's favorite word.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus went on a retreat in the desert.
what it means: straight from the river, the beloved Son is driven into the wilderness; love doesn't mean an easy road.
what a scholar hears: euthys, again and again; schizomenous, the heavens torn, the same verb Mark uses for the temple veil at the end.

notes: The carry 'straightway' is King James wording (Douay uses 'immediately'/'forthwith'), so the KJV is quoted for 1:10 and named; Douay-Rheims 1:12 given from memory. Confirm both.
Count of euthys in Mark: usually given as about 41–42; the script says 'around forty'.
schizō used at 1:10 (heavens torn) and 15:38 (temple veil torn): confirm.
Ekballō ('drove out') at 1:12 is the verb Mark uses for casting out demons: confirm.
The Father's words at 1:11 paraphrased ('you are my beloved Son, in you I am well pleased').
Liturgy: Baptism of the Lord closes Christmastide; Mark 1:12–15 is the First Sunday of Lent, Year B. Confirm.
